deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a fair-copy page of lecture or school notes on ancient Near Eastern history, a continuous German prose text. It continues 'I. Assyrische Geschichte' from the previous page and begins 'II. Medische Monarchie'. Its content, restated:

(1) End of the Assyrian section:
- The Assyrian king (Salmanasser, continued from p.6) took Samaria. This overthrew the kingdom of Israel, and the Hebrews were deported into inner Asia.
- d. Sanherib (Sennacherib) was the most powerful of these kings. About 714 he led a great campaign (against Palestine/Judah and Egypt or Arabia; the word is hard to read). He had to turn back because a great epidemic broke out in his army.
- e. Assarhaddon (Esarhaddon), his youngest son, succeeded him. The notes say the Assyrian empire was overthrown by the Medes under him.

(2) II. Median monarchy:
- We know as little that is certain about it as about the Assyrian monarchy; the sources are in Herodotus.
- The Medes were divided into 6 tribes, one of which, the Magi, formed the priestly caste.
- After 520 years under Assyrian rule the Medes broke away. Their leader was Arbaces.
- The Medes then chose their first king, Dejoces, c. 700. He was a Mede by birth and until then a judge (Schiedsrichter) in a district.
- He built Ekbatana and is said to have introduced court ceremonial. He reigned 53 years.
- His son Phraortes followed, c. 660. He conquered Persis, and through this the Medes first gained preponderance in Asia.
- The page ends mid-narrative (continued on p.8 with Phraortes' death at Nineveh after 22 years).

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. The only numerical content is chronological: dates and reign lengths.
errors: Internal chronological inconsistency: Dejoces is dated c. 700 with a 53-year reign, which puts his successor c. 647, yet Phraortes is dated c. 660 (only 40 years later). The next page's Cyaxares c. 638 is consistent with 660 - 22.

Historical: Sennacherib's major campaign against Judah (with the plague story of 2 Kings 19 and Herodotus II.141) is dated 701 BC, not 714. In 714 Sargon II, who is omitted from the list, was reigning.
Historical: Assyria did not fall under Esarhaddon (d. 669 BC). Nineveh fell in 612 BC under Sin-shar-ishkun to Medes and Babylonians. This conflation reflects older handbook chronology.

Herodotus (I.95) gives 520 years of Assyrian rule over upper Asia and 53 years for Deioces (I.102); these figures are reported correctly. The Arbaces story derives from Ctesias/Diodorus, not Herodotus, so it is mixed tradition.

results.what: Historical lecture notes on Assyrian and Median kings (Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, Deioces, Phraortes) following Herodotus' chronology
results.modern_name: Not mathematics; ancient history school/lecture notes
results.usually_credited_to: Herodotus, Histories I.95-103; standard early-19th-century history textbooks

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical prose about Assyrian and Median history, with no mathematical content. It is likely student or lecture notes, perhaps not even in Gauss's own hand. There is nothing of mathematical-historical significance.

checkable.asserts: If Dejoces began c. 700 BC and reigned 53 years, his reign ends c. 647 BC, not 660 BC as the notes imply.
Phraortes from c. 660 BC with a 22-year reign (next page) gives Cyaxares' accession c. 638 BC, consistent with the next page.
Cyaxares c. 638 BC plus Herodotus' 40-year reign gives Astyages' accession c. 598 BC, matching the next page.
